This isn't surprising at all. Their intent was not to do it properly, it was to do the minimal effort to make money. This is why things like Steam refunds are so valuable, because they tell the publisher just how much money they lost with this common practice.

Can we take a second to go through the cost-benefit analysis a company has to perform in a situation like this? You have invested millions of dollars and probably years in a game. You're made aware of the fact that the game runs less than perfectly, but you're too close to release date to fix the issues. Your options are to...

  • Scrap the whole project because it didn't work out - waste all of the money and time that you put into it.

  • Delay release date, receive negative press and render your carefully crafted marketing plan far less effective. Invest more money and time to fix problems, while likely selling fewer units because of consumer frustration over the delay (i.e. put more money into a project that is already going to face diminished returns).

  • Release the game on-time, despite problems, capitalize on the hype your marketing campaign has created, plan to patch game after release to preserve consumer confidence in your ability/willingness to support your product.

A company exists to make money - if they don't make money, our economic system will cause them to die. Can any of us really blame them for choosing the 3rd option, which gives them the greatest chance to earn money on something they've already dumped millions of dollars into? Option 1 is never going to happen, and option 2 essentially ruins all of their sales projections and forces them to invest more money in the game, and raises expectations to the point of, "they delayed release, so when it comes out it better be absolutely flawless."

In this day and age, with Let's Plays and other reviews to readily available through Youtube and the like, why would you not just wait a day or two, watch a reviewer you trust, then make your buying decision?

Disclaimer - I don't want to defend Warner Bros., I just want people to understand that they can avoid wasting money on broken garbage with just a bit of due diligence. On this, I very much take the same position as James Willems from Funhaus:

...we respect all of you enough to tell you that these companies have STDs, and you should use a condom if you want to fuck them. But you can't come back at us with gonorrhea all over your butthole and get pissed when we propose that maybe this is partly your fault. ... We trust you to be a safe consumer, but we won't put your condom on for you.

An Everyday Linux User Review Of Debian Jessie
Debian is primarily a server OS for professionals. If one finds the desktop user experience lacking I wouldn't necessarily put any weight on it.

A thorough lack of research and analysis. There are excellent reasons why experienced Debianistas recommend distros other than Debian to naive users. This review would have conveyed significant frustration had Newell installed on a laptop with wifi requiring non-free firmware - arguably the most common use case for single-user systems. The "easy-to-use" distros based on Debian make sensible compromises, but nonetheless surrender basic Debian commitments to choice and freedom..

"The installer is a little bit convoluted"

I stopped reading the article right there. If he has problems with a modern Debian feed-in-a-disk-and-click type install, l'm done reading.

I have Jessie installed on a laptop I use part of the time. It's absolutely fine. The user experience is only lacking for me in one way: Jessie broke the hibernate function on this particular laptop. It worked fine on wheezy, so I'm sure there's a fix for it, but I can't be bothered to sort it.

Yeah I don't really agree with this guy. I'm a basic end-user running Debian as my only OS so take that into account when reading this perspective.

I switched from Windows 8.1 because of all the under-the-hood shit that's beyond user control. Mainly updates and weird hdd writing at seemingly random times. Also my internet was fucked for a bit and I got wireshark to see if anyone was borrowing anything. I don't claim to know shit about this but there's enough info out there to make surface level operations accessible. Found that my vanilla 8.1 was making secure connections to some ip in santa monica that was registered to a market research company. Looool, fuck that.

Ubuntu/Mint is the usual choice but not an option for anyone who's read and cares about the data collection thing. Fedora is funded by Red Hat, Debian is not funded. Mainly the transparent ethics and how Debian got started made the decision for me. Switched from Jessie to Stretch a few weeks ago. Only issue so far is Iceweasel occasionally gets bogged down when a fuckton of tabs are open for whatever reason.

Now onto this user review. The intro was irksome and I'm gonna vent. The rest is just the author saying "it basically works."

the website is hard to navigate

I found the downloads to stable releases and documentation on how to install without issue. There's no flashy CSS or whatever makes colorful buttons and that's fine by me. Getting to unstable releases forced me to use an external search engine but by making something like that too easy to find you're just inviting negative feedback from lazy users.

As for installation methods, they're basically self-explanatory. I went for cd isos booted from a usb. Disk 1 will do the whole thing by downloading necessary files from whatever repository you select. All the other disks are for a fully offline install afaik. How did I figure this out? By doing a very basic internet search. Less than two minutes to find and read short explanations on each method of installation.

I couldn't get the live USB to boot with UEFI

Legit complaint, Microsoft is being a shit with this new thing (partition table?) and a lot of distros are having a headache with this apparently. But I got Debian to boot/install/run with UEFI and SecureBoot enabled through the entire fucking process. This took some research and honest to god learning to get through. If you can turn off secureboot then great, fuck it. If you can't you need a signed .efi file (i.e. copy the one from ubuntu or mint's live cd) stuck in the efi or boot folder on your install disk. Had I been able to find that last sentence easily, I would have been able to save some time and learning. Most of the methods out there didn't work for me though, just this one.

Having spent so much time learning about it makes me want to learn how to write .efi files to help fix issues. I like that working through a problem made me want to learn more and contribute. Never happens with Windows.

The installer is a little bit convoluted with similar option spread over a number of screens

Nope. Just because all options are removed from the Windows installation doesn't mean that actually seeing what's going on is redundant. Let's look at it like ordering a burger from two types of establishments. Debian installer gives you options, Windows makes it easy.

Debian installer: What bread would you like for the bun? Toasted? How well done would you like the patty? Cheese? What kind? Sauce? What kind; the options are ketchup, mustard, mayo, bbq, thousand island, a1? Tomatoes? Lettuce? Onions? Bacon? ... *burger is made according to instructions.

Windows installer: *standard "burger" is made based on availability of cheap ingredients and cook's mood.

Is the former convoluted with repetitive options? You could argue that Debian's asking you how you want your burger over and over but that'd basically be dishonest. If someone's never had a burger, maybe they would prefer going to Windows over googling what a tomato is. Hopefully they don't end up thinking the Windows burger is as good as it gets.

tl;dr Debian is an excellent choice even if you're Linux naive. Ignore everydaylinuxuser.
